scoreRule: 1 point per correct MC item; 10 points maximum; local provisional grade only
description: Independently authored EN/C1 review-comprehension test draft. External linguistic and didactic audit pending.

tabs.title: Evidence and evaluation
tabs.description: Evaluate what the reviewer supports and questions.

tabs.title: Critical transfer
tabs.description: Apply the review's argument in new contexts.

questions.q: What contrast does the opening paragraph establish?
choices: The reviewer believes documentaries should never evoke emotion.
A concern about recycling is less important than camera technique.
The film makes viewers feel responsible before helping them understand practical solutions.
Litter is too small a subject to deserve serious film-making.
questions.explanation: The wrapper scene generates a strong emotional judgement before the film has explained what action might follow.

questions.q: Why are the beautiful images of the cleaners described as having a double effect?
choices: They highlight labour but risk turning workers' conditions into an aesthetic spectacle.
They make the square look dirtier than it really is.
They establish working conditions more clearly than interviews could.
They contradict the earlier image of an empty square.
questions.explanation: The reviewer praises the visual detail while noting how little the audience learns about workers' agency or conditions.

questions.q: What broader issue may be implied by the cleaner's observation that the square is cleanest when nobody sees it?
choices: The film crew could not find the cleaner's name.
Night cleaning is more expensive than daytime cleaning.
Viewers should avoid using public squares after concerts.
Essential work is often invisible to the people who benefit from it.
questions.explanation: The remark points to unseen labour and the social invisibility of those doing it.

questions.q: Why does the facilities manager's interview change the reviewer's view of the film?
choices: It establishes that deposit schemes should be abandoned.
It allows the complexity of a proposed solution to remain visible rather than reducing it to good intentions.
It reveals that the manager opposes all environmental measures.
It proves that spreadsheets are more appealing than cinema.
questions.explanation: The manager details storage, training and washing costs without dismissing the goal.

questions.q: How does the repeated slow-motion shot of the teenager affect the documentary's argument?
choices: It proves that the teenager is solely responsible for the town's waste.
It helps viewers understand the difficulties faced by cleaning staff.
It shifts attention from systems and infrastructure to the guilt of an individual.
It provides a balanced comparison with the manager's interview.
questions.explanation: The repeated image redirects a structural problem into a moralised individual scene.

questions.q: Why does the reviewer discuss who is named, explained or shown only as a silhouette?
choices: The narrator should provide the full names of all visitors.
The filmmaker has accidentally forgotten some production credits.
The film needs more characters to hold the audience's attention.
The distinction affects the meaning and agency assigned to each person on screen.
questions.explanation: The film's unequal treatment of cleaners, manager and teenager functions as an argument through representation.

questions.q: Why does the volunteer's admission about extra washing trips strengthen rather than weaken the reusable-cup case?
choices: It makes improvement open to evidence and revision instead of unqualified praise.
It shows the idea never should have been tested.
It proves that the first event was already cheaper than disposable cups.
It gives the director an opportunity for a more dramatic soundtrack.
questions.explanation: The reviewer finds an honest account of unforeseen costs more credible than a spotless success narrative.

questions.q: An environmental campaign proposes reusable cups but says nothing about where they will be washed. What is missing?
choices: A promise that all guests will become more responsible.
A sufficiently striking image of a disposable cup.
An operational plan addressing facilities, staffing and actual costs.
A list of celebrities willing to promote the campaign.
questions.explanation: The facilities manager's example insists that logistics are part of the solution.

questions.q: In a film, workers appear only as anonymous silhouettes while managers explain policy in detail. What should a critical viewer ask?
choices: How to reduce the total length of the film.
Whose experience and decision-making power the film makes visible.
Whether the film contains enough music for a broad audience.
Which characters would look best in close-up shots.
questions.explanation: The reviewer treats such representational choices as substantive claims about agency.

questions.q: What would make a school waste-reduction documentary more convincing to this reviewer?
choices: Including evidence of what worked, what failed and what needs to change.
Editing out failed attempts to keep the message positive.
Showing only the neatest moment after an event.
Blaming individual pupils instead of discussing practical arrangements.
questions.explanation: The final paragraph celebrates admitting unexpected consequences and inviting correction.
